Chicken breast has a reputation for coming out dry, but that's rarely bad luck, it's usually one of three fixable habits. 1. Cooking it straight out of the package 📦 A raw chicken breast is naturally tapered, thick on one end and thin on the other, so by the time the thick end finishes cooking, the thin end has been overcooked for several minutes already. Pounding it to an even thickness with a mallet or the bottom of a heavy pan means every part of the breast finishes at the same time, edges included. 2. Skipping the brine 🧂 Salt dissolved in water, or even just salt sitting on the surface, denatures the proteins in the meat and loosens the muscle fibers, which lets them hold onto more water once heat is applied. A quick fifteen to thirty minute soak in salted water, or a dry salt rest if you're short on time, is the difference between chicken that stays juicy and chicken that wrings itself out like a sponge. 3. Cooking it straight to 165 on the heat 🌡️ The USDA's own pasteurization tables show that time and temperature work together, which is why chefs commonly pull chicken breast at 160 and let it rest, since the residual heat carries it up to a safe 165 on its own. Cooking it all the way to 165 while it's still over direct heat means it's already closer to 170 or higher by the time it hits the plate. None of this is complicated, it's just three small adjustments most people skip without realizing it. Which one of these have you been missing 👇🍗 #foodie #chef #cooking #bbq #steak
